set.overview: Silliman is a big granite summit above Lodgepole in Sequoia National Park, climbed by way of a primitive use trail beside Silliman Creek, then open slabs to two high lakes and a sandy, boulder-strewn slope to the top. Nothing is harder than class 2, but the route-finding through brush and over slabs is the real challenge, and the day is long and steep.
set.approach: Start at the Twin Lakes trailhead beside the Lodgepole campground, crossing the Marble Fork on a bridge and climbing the trail for roughly 1.6 miles. At the Silliman Creek crossing, turn off at the sign onto the use trail on the east side of the creek, which leads north to Silliman Meadow. Above the meadow, push through brush to a granite basin of wide slabs, keep right at the creek fork toward Silliman Lake, and carry on past the upper lake to the foot of the summit slope.
set.descent_text: Go back down the way you came: sand and boulders to the upper lake, then the gully and ledges below Silliman Lake, the slabs, the brushy stretch to Silliman Meadow, and the use trail down to the main trail and the campground. The gully looks cliffy from above but has workable paths; follow a track or cairns carefully, since faint branching paths in the brush are easy to lose.
hazards: Faint, branching use trail and heavy brush above Silliman Meadow make route-finding hard, especially on the way down
Steep granite slabs and ledges between the meadow and Silliman Lake
Afternoon thunderstorms build over the lakes; start early
Avalanche path near Silliman Meadow, and steep snow below the lakes in spring

evidence.fact: 16.3 km round trip (10.1 mi) out and back; halved for one-way = 8.13 km

review.notes: Gain skipped: the only guide figure (about 4,420 ft) is below summit 11,188 minus trailhead ~6,720 (4,468 ft), so it fails the possibility check; a personal blog gave 4,866 ft and 13.8 mi round trip, which disagrees with the 10.1 mi guide figure by more than 10 percent. Distance is one source only. Trailhead and junction mileage (1.6 mi) taken from a spring trip report.

set.approach: Start from the Mineral King road end and take the Sawtooth Pass trail toward Glacier Pass, a cross-country notch with a short easy class 3 descent on its far side. From there reach Black Rock Pass and drop to the Little Five Lakes basin, where most parties camp. The climb proper begins at Black Rock Pass, where you leave the trail and gain the ridge running north toward the summit.
set.descent_text: Return along the same ridge to Black Rock Pass, then follow the trail back toward Little Five Lakes camp or on to Mineral King. A quicker way down from Glacier Pass heads southwest straight down the drainage to the old Sawtooth Pass trail near 9,700 feet, which is shorter than the maintained trail.
hazards: Ridge traverse from Black Rock Pass has third-class sections, with buttresses that force detours onto loose sand and steeper rock
Loose rock along the crest and a very long, tiring day if the party returns to camp late
Early in the season an ice band below Glacier Pass can block the crossing without crampons

review.notes: Season, gain, distance skipped: only trip reports from one autumn and one June exist; approaches are multi-day from Mineral King and a one-way trailhead-to-summit figure is not defined. The row line is the ridge from Black Rock Pass; the 1998 report describes a north traverse from that pass.

set.overview: Lippincott Mountain is a 12,265-foot summit on the Great Western Divide in Sequoia National Park, usually climbed from a camp near Little Five Lakes. The standard line is the southeast slope above the Black Rock Pass trail, a bowl of second-class boulders and sand that leads to the ridge, with a few third-class moves near the top.
set.approach: Start at Mineral King and climb the Sawtooth Pass trail to Glacier Pass, then continue over Black Rock Pass to the Little Five Lakes basin, about 10 to 11 miles with over 5,000 feet of climbing, so most parties camp. Leave the Big Arroyo trail after crossing a shoulder near 10,400 feet, contour to the north shore of the lake at 10,295 feet, and go on to the higher lake at 10,800 feet beneath the east face.
set.descent_text: Come down the way you went up: the sand and boulder bowl to the higher lake, then the trail back to camp or over Black Rock Pass. On the way out, a drainage that heads southwest from Glacier Pass reaches the old Sawtooth Pass trail near 9,700 feet and shortens the walk to Mineral King.
hazards: Long approach with two high passes; a late return to camp is common
Ice on the north side of Glacier Pass early in the season may need crampons, and snow can turn parties back
Some third-class moves on the upper slope, with loose boulders and sand

review.notes: Distance and season skipped: trailhead-to-summit is multi-day and no neutral one-way figure found; the user-logged GPS day figures are not evidence. Stored gain 8,405 ft left alone.

set.overview: Antichrist Dihedral is a tall, sustained line of about nine long pitches on the north-facing Main Wall of Mount Stewart, above the Lilliput Glacier in Sequoia National Park. It follows crack and corner systems to a big dihedral, with a steep roof and delicate protection on the upper wall, in a remote setting with a long walk in.
hazards: Steep roof and thin protection on the upper dihedral; micro nuts are needed
Wall is taller than it looks, so a late top-out and a descent by headlamp are likely
Descent by rappel and scrambling needs gear to build or back up anchors
Long remote approach with no quick way out

review.notes: Grade conflict: Mountain Project lists 5.10c while the first-ascent article says IV 5.11b, about 1,600 feet; not changed (grade not in fill). Season, gain and distance skipped: only an August 2018 first ascent and a 16-mile walk to Tamarack Lake were found; gain not stated.

set.overview: Lion Rock is a 12,360-foot peak on the Great Western Divide in Sequoia National Park, reached from the north by way of Triple Divide Pass and the Lion Lakes. The unroped way up is on the south side, a class 2 route through a maze of chutes and buttresses, long and complicated rather than hard.
set.approach: Start from Rowell Meadow, reached by a one-lane road off the Lodgepole road. Hike via Sugarloaf Meadow and the Roaring River to Cloud Canyon and Glacier Lake, then cross Triple Divide Pass and drop to the Lion Lakes. From there climb a chute to the east ridge, descend into the southeast bowl, and gain the south ridge.
set.descent_text: Go back down by the ascent route: through the buttresses and chutes of the south ridge, across the southeast bowl and east ridge chute to the Lion Lakes, then up over Triple Divide Pass and out past Glacier Lake and Cloud Canyon.
hazards: Chute below the east ridge can hold snow into August and needs care
Intricate maze of chutes and buttresses on the south ridge makes route-finding hard
Long up-and-down day with a pass crossing at each end

review.notes: Single trip report (August 2003). Distance and season skipped: no mileage or season stated. Stored gain 7,650 ft left alone.

set.overview: Mount Kaweah is a 13,802-foot summit in Sequoia National Park, reached from Mineral King across two high passes and the Big Arroyo, then by a cross-country climb from the High Sierra Trail. The final slope is loose scree and talus to a saddle, then a rib and the summit ridge, where the first high point is a false summit and the true top is about a quarter mile beyond.
set.approach: Start at the Timber Gap trailhead at Mineral King and take the old use trail over Glacier Pass to Spring Lake, then Hands and Knees Pass and the Little Five Lakes basin. Descend to the Big Arroyo and the High Sierra Trail junction near 9,550 feet, then leave the trail and climb an off-trail rib to the Mount Kaweah and Second Kaweah saddle.
set.descent_text: Return along the summit ridge to the saddle, picking out sandy patches in the scree where possible, then drop to the High Sierra Trail at the Big Arroyo. Go back out by the same route over Hands and Knees Pass and Glacier Pass, which is a long climb on the return.
hazards: Loose scree and talus on the final slope below the summit ridge
Class 3 gullies on the Glacier Pass descent toward Spring Lake can cliff out in the dark
Steep granite slabs near Spring Lake force awkward sidehilling at lake level
Streams in the Big Arroyo can run very low late in the season

review.notes: One trip report only (30.1 mi round trip, user-logged); distance skipped because a personal GPS figure is not evidence and no second source. Season skipped (report written late fall, date unclear). Stored gain left alone.

set.overview: The Southwest Chute is the usual way up Black Kaweah, a dark volcanic peak on the Great Western Divide in Sequoia National Park. From the base of the main chute, sustained and difficult class 3 climbing leads up the gully to the West Ridge, then a right-leaning ramp reaches the summit, with some class 4 if you stray from the line.
set.approach: Start at Mineral King and hike north of Monarch Creek toward Glacier Pass, then Spring Lake, Hands and Knees Pass, Little Five Lakes, and down to the Big Arroyo. Leave the trail at the Kaweah Gap junction and climb cross-country through forest past a tarn southwest of the summit, over slabs and a talus fan, to the base of the right-hand chute and the main chute.
set.descent_text: Descend the main chute and the right-hand chute, following the cairns; at the top of the ramp an alternate way off is mostly class 3 with a steep class 4 chimney at the bottom. Then retrace the approach to the Big Arroyo and back over the passes to Mineral King.
hazards: Loose dark volcanic rock in the chutes, with rockfall risk for anyone below
Route-finding: cairns can lure parties onto harder class 4 ground
Loose class 3 descent from Glacier Pass on the way back, harder by headlamp
Climb takes longer than it looks from below

review.notes: Single trip report (Sept 2006). Gain and distance skipped: only a round-trip full-route total (about 26 mi, 11,000 ft), a trip-report figure with no second source. Season skipped: one September date only.

set.overview: Picket Guard Peak is a 12,302-foot summit west of the Sierra crest in Sequoia National Park, among the hardest of the Sierra Peaks to reach. The standard route is the class 2 east ridge, reached from the Kern-Kaweah drainage, with a third-class summit block at the very top.
set.approach: There is no short way in. From the Shepherd Pass trailhead, hike down the upper Kern to Junction Meadow and on to a camp in the Kern-Kaweah drainage near Rockslide Lake. From Mineral King the alternative is over Glacier Pass, Black Rock Pass, Little Five Lakes and Kaweah Pass. From camp, ford the Kern-Kaweah River and climb steep wooded slopes to the east ridge.
set.descent_text: Return by the east ridge and the same wooded slopes to the river crossing and camp. A break at Picket Guard Lake on the way down is common. Allow plenty of time, since the way back out of the Kern-Kaweah country is long.
hazards: Kern-Kaweah River must be forded with boots off on the way in and out
Steep wooded slopes below the east ridge, with willows and talus hopping on the cross-country sections
Loose rock and a steep band on the Kaweah Pass descent if approached from Mineral King
Summit block is third class

review.notes: Gain, distance, season skipped: multi-day approach from two possible trailheads, only user-logged day totals.

set.overview: Kern Point is a 12,730-foot summit above the Kern-Kaweah drainage in Sequoia National Park. The standard line is a class 2 climb up granite slabs on the west-facing slope, reached from a camp after a long walk down the upper Kern, with a fairly long day on the peak itself.
set.approach: Start at the Shepherd Pass trailhead and hike down the upper Kern River to Junction Meadow, crossing the broad river near the meadow. Follow the Colby Pass trail, faint in many places, for about a half mile, then leave it and climb the granite slabs of the northwest slope toward the summit.
set.descent_text: Come down by a line slightly north of the one you went up; the paths on the slope are all much alike. Return to the Colby Pass trail and the camp in the Kern-Kaweah country, then walk out to Shepherd Pass trailhead.
hazards: Kern River crossing near Junction Meadow where the river spreads wide
Steep granite slabs on the way up and down are hard on feet and tendons
Faint trail along Colby Pass route and heavy mosquitoes at low camps in early summer

review.notes: One trip report; distance and season skipped. Report calls the slope northwest while the row says standard route; hedged. Stored gain 11,020 left alone.

set.overview: Triple Divide Peak is a 12,634-foot summit in Sequoia National Park where three watersheds meet. A party climbed it by the crest, up the west ridge and down the east ridge, in a long loop; the ridge is a hard class 3 with one or two class 4 moves, harder than its class 2 listing suggests.
set.approach: Start from Rowell Meadow, reached by a one-lane road off the Lodgepole road. Hike through Sugarloaf Meadow and along the Roaring River into Cloud Canyon, continuing to Glacier Lake. From the lake, climb toward the west ridge and follow its crest to the summit.
set.descent_text: Descend the east ridge, staying on or near the crest, and return to the Glacier Lake and Cloud Canyon trail. Another line, from Triple Divide Pass, stays on the face and climbs a last buttress.
hazards: The crest is a hard class 3 with one or two class 4 moves
Rockfall from the north face, including after small earthquakes
Long approach through Cloud Canyon makes it a multi-day trip

review.notes: One trip report (Aug 2003); describes a crest traverse, not necessarily the class 2 line the row lists. Gain, distance, season skipped, no figures. Row grade (Class 2) conflicts with the report's hard class 3.
